blocks.prompt: The Last Mile
blocks.text: Look around your room. The bed. The lamp. The shoes by the door. Almost every one of those things rode on a truck to get here. Ships and trains carry things a long way. But a ship cannot pull up to your street. A train cannot stop at your store. So a truck does the last part of the trip. Drivers call that part the last mile. A full truck can weigh as much as twenty cars. It has a bed behind the seats, so the driver can sleep, wake up, and keep going.

blocks.prompt: Why an 18 Wheeler Has Two Halves
blocks.text: Count the wheels on a big rig and you get eighteen. Two at the front, eight under the middle, eight at the back. But look closer and you will see something stranger. The truck is not one machine. It is two. The front half is called the tractor. That is where the engine is, and the driver, and a small bed for sleeping. The back half is the trailer, and it is really just a box on wheels. It has no engine. It has no front wheels at all. The front of the trailer rests on the back of the tractor, on a heavy steel plate shaped like a horseshoe. Drivers call that plate the fifth wheel. A thick pin under the trailer drops into it and locks. That one joint is why a truck can bend around a corner instead of tipping. It is also why a driver can unhook one trailer, leave it at a store, and hook up a new one in a few minutes. The tractor keeps working. The trailer waits its turn.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Trucks stop with air, not fluid

Air pressure holds them open

blocks.prompt: The Brakes That Work by Letting Go
blocks.text: Stand near a truck stop and you will hear it. A loud hiss, every time a rig pulls away. That sound is a truck doing something a car never does. It is releasing its brakes with air. A car stops with liquid. Push the pedal, and brake fluid pushes on the wheels. It works well, but every drop of that fluid has to stay inside the line. Spring a serious leak and the pedal goes soft under your foot. A truck weighing forty tons cannot take that chance, so trucks stop with air instead, and they use it backward. Here is how. Inside each brake sits a heavy coiled spring. The spring has one job: clamp the brake shut. To let the truck roll at all, the engine pumps compressed air into the brake chamber, and that air shoves the spring back and pins it there. The whole time a truck is rolling down the highway, air pressure is fighting a spring to hold the brakes open. Now think about what happens if an air line snaps. The air escapes. Nothing is holding the spring anymore. The spring does what springs do, and the brakes slam on. A broken truck stops itself. Engineers call this a fail safe: when the system breaks, it breaks toward safety instead of away from it. So that hiss at the truck stop is the sound of a driver giving forty tons of steel permission to move.

notes: Diesel engines have no spark plugs

blocks.prompt: The Engine With No Spark
blocks.text: Pop the hood of a car and you will find spark plugs, one for each cylinder, firing a small electric spark to light the fuel. Pop the hood of a truck and there are none. A diesel engine has no spark plugs, because it does not need a spark. It lights its fuel with pressure alone. Here is the trick. Squeeze any gas hard enough and it gets hot. A bicycle pump warms in your hand for the same reason. A diesel engine takes a cylinder of ordinary air and crushes it into roughly one twentieth of the space it started in. By the top of that stroke the air has climbed past 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit, hot enough that when the injector sprays in a fine mist of fuel, the fuel catches on contact. No spark. No plug. Just pressure and heat. Rudolf Diesel built the first working engine of this kind in Germany in the 1890s. He was chasing efficiency, and he found it. Squeezing the air harder wrings more work out of every drop of fuel, which is why almost every truck, ship, train, and tractor on Earth still runs on his idea more than a century later. That efficiency comes with a personality. A diesel makes enormous pulling power, but only across a narrow band of speeds. A car engine will happily spin to 6,000 revolutions a minute. A big truck engine does its best work below 2,000, and it has to stay inside that band while hauling forty tons up a hill. The answer is gears, and lots of them. Where a family car has six, a highway truck may have ten, thirteen, or eighteen, and the driver climbs through them like rungs on a ladder. All that mass has one more consequence, and it is the one that matters most. A car at highway speed needs roughly 300 feet to stop. A fully loaded truck at the same speed needs closer to 525 feet, nearly two football fields of road. Getting forty tons moving is clever engineering. Getting it stopped is the hard part.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Malcom McLean: trucker turned shipping owner
The Ideal X sailed April 26, 1956
58 boxes, Newark to Houston
Loading cost fell from $5.86 to about $0.16 a ton
Container width matches a highway trailer
The twistlock patent was released royalty free

blocks.prompt: The Truck Driver Who Shrank the World
blocks.text: The story Malcom McLean told for the rest of his life begins in 1937, with a young North Carolina trucker sitting at a pier in Hoboken, New Jersey, going nowhere. He had hauled a load of cotton bales up from the south, and now he watched dockworkers pull those bales off his trailer one at a time, carry them across the pier, sling them in a net, and lower them into a ship's hold, where another crew stacked them by hand. It took most of a day. McLean was not paid to sit. And sitting there, he had the thought that would eventually rearrange the global economy: why unload the cargo at all? Why not lift the whole box? Nobody wanted that idea for the next eighteen years. Ports were built around the old way. Shipping lines owned the warehouses the old way filled. Dockworkers' unions were built on the labor the old way demanded, and they could see precisely what a box would do to it. In 1956, loading a ship cost roughly $5.86 for every ton moved, and almost none of that was fuel or steel. It was people, lifting things. McLean did not wait for permission. By 1955 he had grown McLean Trucking into one of the largest fleets in America, and he sold the entire thing. With the money he bought a struggling steamship company, cut the decks out of an old oil tanker, and bolted steel frames on top of it. On April 26, 1956, that ship, the Ideal X, sailed from Newark to Houston carrying fifty eight truck trailer boxes. When the accountants ran the numbers on the voyage, loading had cost about sixteen cents a ton. The old way cost roughly thirty six times as much. The genius was not really the box. Boxes are easy. The genius was insisting the box be identical everywhere. McLean's engineer, Keith Tantlinger, designed a corner fitting and a twistlock that let a crane grab any container, and let containers stack and lock to each other on a ship, on a railcar, or on a chassis behind a truck. Then McLean did the thing that decided the whole story: he gave the patent away, royalty free, so that every one of his rivals could copy it. A standard that only one company is allowed to use is not a standard. It is a cage. What followed was not an improvement in shipping. It was a reordering. Freight costs fell so far that they stopped being a serious factor in where a thing gets made, which is a large part of why the shirt you are wearing was probably sewn on the other side of an ocean. Ports that could not handle containers, including some of the busiest on Earth, simply died, and new ones rose out of mudflats where there was room for cranes and truck lanes. Waterfronts full of jobs vanished. Whole industries appeared. And through all of it, the truck never left. A shipping container is 8 feet wide for a reason that has nothing to do with ships: that is how wide a highway trailer is. The box that crosses the Pacific was shaped to fit behind a diesel tractor on an American road, because the man who invented it was thinking, always, like a trucker stuck on a dock. Ships carry containers across oceans. Trains carry them across continents. But nothing on Earth can put one on your street except a truck. Every supply chain, however long, ends the way it began in 1937: with a driver, a trailer, and somebody waiting on the box.
